Five grouting methods – what does the grout do to the soil?

In grouting, a binder is injected into the pores, fissures and voids of the soil or rock through drilled or driven pipes. Reducing the void volume improves the strength and deformation properties. In mass stabilisation, the soil is mixed in place with a binder.

Low-viscosity, fast-setting grout is injected at high pressure through “forced” fractures in soils and rocks. Grout sheets form in the opening fractures, and the ground rises together with the structure above it. Injection through sleeved pipes can be repeated several times, so the movement can be controlled precisely.

At higher pressure, small voids are formed stage by stage and filled with the injected stiff grout. The grout does not penetrate the pores: it displaces and compacts the surrounding looser soil. The bulbs forming one above the other create load-bearing columns.
strengthening loose sand before tunnelling or excavation
cut-off curtain under an excavation or a dam
low-viscosity material: cement grout, microfine cement, water-glass based or resin solution

At low pressure, the voids between the grains are filled without disturbing the soil structure. The void volume does not change; only the voids are filled. Grouting proceeds in stages from the bottom upwards as the pipe is withdrawn; the injected volume and the pressure are monitored continuously.
